newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Exiled Cambodian prince to press to go home.
newsitem.headline: Exiled Cambodian prince to press to go home.

text.p: Exiled Prince Norodom Sirivudh, accused of plotting to kill Cambodian co-Premier Hun Sen, was barred from returning to Cambodia on Tuesday but said he would persist in attempts to go home for a fair trial.
Sirivudh, stranded in Hong Kong when an airline refused to fly him home after warnings he would be arrested, said his government had nothing to fear as he had no army behind him.
"I will ask the Hong Kong authorities to allow me to find a solution to go back home," the prince told a news conference at Hong Kong airport.

"I'm still a member of parliament and ask not for a violent solution, but just a review of my trial.... I accept to be in jail, to be under house arrest. That's how I ask to review my trial case. I'm ready for this," he told reporters.

Sirivudh, travelling on a Cambodian diplomatic passport, had been issued a boarding pass by Hong Kong airline Dragonair for a 4.40 p.m. (0840 GMT) flight to Phnom Penh. He was later refused access after Cambodian authorities told the airline the prince would be arrested in Phnom Penh.

A half brother of King Norodom Sihanouk and a former foreign minister, Sirivudh went into exile in December 1995 after being held for one month on charges of involvement in an alleged plot against the life of Second Prime Minister Hun Sen.

The prince, who arrived in the British colony from Frankfurt on Tuesday, has denied the charges and said he wanted to return home to seek justice after being sentenced to 10 years jail in absentia over the alleged plot.
Visibly weary, the prince, said on Tuesday Dragonair had been threatened.

"The representative of Dragonair said clearly in front of Hong Kong authorities that they received threats from the Royal government to put in danger all carrier flights who try to fly to Cambodia (with) me on board," he told reporters.
A Dragonair spokesman told Reuters earlier that Cambodian consulate officials in Hong Kong had informed the airline that Phnom Penh had forbidden the prince to land.

Co-Interior Minister You Hockry said earlier on Tuesday Sirivudh would be arrested on arrival. "If he arrives he will be taken to T3 (prison in Phnom Penh). That's what we plan to do," You Hockry said.

You Hockry said he had discussed the issue on Sunday with his co-minister Sar Kheng of Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party (CPP), which formed an uneasy coalition with the royalist FUNCINPEC party after U.N.-run elections in 1993.
"Sirivudh must come with a pardon. Without a royal pardon FUCNINPEC cannot do much legally," said the minister, a royalist.
But Sirivudh dismissed the need for a pardon.
"It's not important to get amnesty because my choice is to go back home even if that means going to jail or house arrest."
King Sihanouk said last week he was not ready to anger Hun Sen by granting an amnesty and warned he would abdicate immediately if the Sirivudh affair was settled by violence.
Sirivudh declared his intentions were non-violent.
"I don't have an army. I'm just a member of parliament fighting for democracy, human rights. I fight for an ideal, not with weapons," he said.
The prince, who will be in Hong Kong for several days, said he will try to book a Royal Air Cambodge flight and will fight to go home as a "Cambodian citizen".
The Cambodian national flag carrier's next flight from Hong Kong to Phnom Penh is on Thursday afternoon, according to a schedule. It was not clear if Sirivudh would be allowed aboard.
